threads.thread_goal: Align on scope, roles and overall move schedule before work starts.

messages.text: Kicking off the Warehouse Move and Metal Line Reconfiguration project here. Scope is to relocate the warehouse inventory and the metal drawing line to the new layout over two consecutive weekends, with no safety incidents and no damage. I have drafted the first version of the move schedule and equipment booking in the sheet linked as Move Schedule and Equipment Booking Sheet, which maps to A1 and covers T2. It breaks the move into two weekend windows, with pre-staging during weekdays. Before we lock anything, we need to confirm the weekend windows, shared forklift and crane slots, and who is coordinating on-site each window. @326777, your input on the metal line downtime and restart is key so we can align A1 with T6 and T8. @534242 and @323962, please check if the layout mapping from T1 matches what you see on the floor.

I went through the draft in A1 and compared it with the current and target layout from T1. The new metal line position and the high-turnover pallet zones look consistent with what we marked on the floor last week. For the weekend windows, the sheet shows first window on the 9th–10th and second on the 16th–17th. From a moving standpoint, that works for me as long as we can lock in two forklifts and one truck for both Saturdays, plus a crane for the metal line on the first Sunday. I flagged those time slots in A1 under T2. @326777, can you confirm if shutting the metal line down Saturday 9th at 14:00 and having it back up by Sunday 10th at 14:00 is realistic with your T6 and T8 steps?

Thanks for laying that out. Looking at A1 and the shutdown and startup procedure in A5, plus the draft steps I put under T6 and T8, a 24-hour window from Saturday 14:00 to Sunday 14:00 is tight but doable if we avoid extra waits on lifting equipment. I would need about 3 hours for controlled shutdown and securing, 4 hours for disconnect and loading, 4 hours for positioning and reconnecting, and 3 hours for checks and test runs. That leaves some buffer for small delays. One concern: if the crane is delayed, we lose that buffer quickly. Can we add a backup slot for the crane in A1, maybe Sunday morning as a contingency, and note that in T2?

I checked the layout part of T1 on the sheet. For the pallet racking near the new metal line, I see we plan to put mixed fast-mover pallets in the first two aisles. That is fine for access, but during the move we will have a lot of temporary staging. In A1 under T2, can we add a note that we keep one aisle fully clear as a corridor for the metal line move and only stage pallets on the opposite side? That should help avoid blocking the crane and forklifts when we are moving the machines.

I went through A1 quickly. For the first weekend, I am down to support packing and loading in the old warehouse zones. I did not fully follow how the time buffers work between the inventory pre-count and the actual loading. Do we have a clear cut-off in T2 for when we stop normal picking and start only move activities on those aisles? If not, I suggest we add a simple rule in A1, like last picks from affected aisles by Friday 16:00 before each weekend.

Good catch on the cut-off. I just updated A1 under T2 with a proposed rule: for each weekend window, last regular picks from affected aisles by Friday 16:00, then we switch those aisles to move-only. That should also help T5 when we do the pre-move stock count. On the crane buffer, I added a contingency slot Sunday 08:00–10:00 as @326777 suggested. Before we lock D1, can everyone confirm that the two weekend dates and the 24-hour metal line window work from your side? If there are any conflicts with other warehouse or production activities, we will need to escalate to the warehouse supervisor and production manager to adjust.

From my side the dates and the 24-hour window are fine. The buffers you added in A1 for crane and forklifts look reasonable. I also like the clear switch from picking to move-only on Fridays; that will make it easier to keep track of what is already counted for T5. I suggest we also note in T1 that the new metal line area stays free of any non-related pallets until after T8 is completed, so we do not have to reshuffle during test runs.

I confirm the 14:00 Saturday to 14:00 Sunday window for the metal line works for me, based on the steps in A5 and the plan in T6 and T8. The extra crane buffer in A1 reduces the risk of overruns. I will coordinate with the maintenance technician to validate the disconnection and reconnection timings, but I do not expect major changes. If they see any issue, I will bring it back here before the first weekend.

Dates and windows work for me too. I will focus on the first weekend pre-staging and loading according to T2. One question: who is taking the lead on-site each weekend? It would help to know who we go to for quick decisions if something in A1 needs to shift during the day.

I am ok with the dates and the Friday 16:00 cut-off. For coordination, I can support but I am not comfortable taking the lead on the whole window, especially if we need to re-plan equipment bookings in A1 on the fly. I would rather have one of you who has been closer to T1 and T2 own that and I can handle a sub-area like the dangerous goods aisle or the mixed pallets zone.

I can take on-site coordination for the first weekend. I know the details in A1 and T2 well enough to adjust sequence and equipment slots if we hit small delays, and I will keep the warehouse supervisor in the loop for any bigger changes. For the second weekend, I can support but it might be better if someone else leads so we are not dependent on one person for both windows.

Thanks for stepping up. I can lead coordination on-site for the second weekend. That way, for weekend one, @534242 is the main point of contact, and for weekend two, it is me. @326777, during the metal line move window, you will be the go-to for any decisions related to T6 and T8 steps, while we handle the general warehouse flow.

Confirmed, I will be on-site and available for any decisions around the metal line shutdown, securing, positioning and test runs, following A5 and the plans in T6 and T8. If something impacts the 24-hour window, I will flag it immediately so we can adjust the sequence in A1 and avoid overruns.

Given all confirmations, I propose we formally approve the overall move schedule in A1: two weekend windows on the 9th–10th and 16th–17th, with the metal line shutdown from Saturday 14:00 to Sunday 14:00 on the first weekend, including the buffers and cut-offs we documented under T2. Unless anyone objects today, we will treat this as the baseline schedule and share it with the warehouse supervisor, production manager and logistics coordinator.

No objections from me. The schedule in A1 covers the main constraints and gives us clear time boxes for each block of work in T2. Once you share it with the stakeholders, we should ask them to confirm equipment availability and flag any conflicts by tomorrow so we still have time to tweak.
Works for me as well. Having the two weekends and the 24-hour metal line window fixed in A1 helps me plan staffing and pre-staging. I will align my tasks under T2 with that baseline.
All good from my side. The Friday 16:00 cut-off and the clear weekend windows in A1 are easy to follow. I will plan my support shifts around that.

Ok, with no objections, we consider the overall move schedule and weekend windows in A1 approved. I will circulate the link to the warehouse supervisor, production manager and logistics coordinator and note the on-site leads for each weekend. Next step is to refine the detailed steps in T2 and make sure T1 is fully up to date with the final layout.

threads.thread_goal: Define and agree on packing, labeling and inventory procedures.

messages.text: I have a question on how we want to label mixed pallets and machine parts for the new layout. When I look at the draft Packing and Labeling Standards Guide in A2 for T4, it is clear for single-SKU pallets, but I am not sure how to handle pallets that combine different SKUs going to different new zones, or crates with metal line parts that need to land exactly by each machine. Also, for the pre-move inventory in A4 under T5, how strict is the cut-off for finishing counts before we start wrapping and moving? I want to avoid re-counting the same pallet twice.

On mixed pallets, my suggestion is we avoid mixing destinations as much as possible. For the cases where we cannot, A2 could define a rule: one main label for the pallet with the primary destination zone, and secondary labels for the extra SKUs with their final bin locations. For machine parts, I would go with a different color and a clear reference to the machine ID and side, so when we reinstall per T8 we know exactly where each crate goes. We can add examples in A2 under T4. For the inventory cut-off in A4 and T5, I think we should set a fixed time the day before each move window when counts must be done and frozen.

I updated A2 with a draft label format: zone code, aisle, bay, and sequence number, plus a short text for content. For color coding, I proposed: yellow for standard inventory pallets, blue for mixed pallets, and red for metal line parts. For mixed pallets, as @534242 said, we try to keep one destination per pallet; if not possible, we list secondary destinations on the same label. For machine parts, red labels will include machine ID and whether it is left, right, or central section, to support T8. On the inventory side, A4 already has columns for old and new locations; we can add a status field to mark when a pallet is counted and sealed so we do not touch it again before the move.

For the metal line parts, the red label idea in A2 works well. If we include the machine ID and section, plus a simple drawing or code for orientation, it will speed up reassembly during T8. I will add a short note in A5 so the shutdown procedure under T6 tells us exactly how to group and label parts when we disconnect them. That way, A2, A4 and A5 stay consistent.

I like the color coding, it is easy to see on the floor. One thing I am not clear on: for blue mixed pallets, if we have items going to two different new zones, do we still move the pallet as one unit and then split it at the new warehouse, or do we split it before loading? I am asking because for T5 and A4, it might be simpler to count them separately before we wrap them.

Good point. To keep inventory clean in A4 and avoid confusion during T9 later, I suggest we split pallets by destination before loading whenever possible. So blue labels would mainly be for cases where we temporarily mix but still have a single final zone. If a pallet truly has two final zones, we should break it into two pallets and label them separately. I can add that rule into A2 under T4.

Splitting by destination before loading makes sense to me. It will make it easier when we do the post-move checks in T9 as well. On the label format, I tested printing a few samples from A2 and they are readable from a distance. I would just keep the text short so we do not spend too much time writing while packing.

I have now updated A2 with the final draft: yellow for standard pallets, blue for single-destination mixed pallets, red for metal line parts, with the label fields we discussed. For pallets with multiple final zones, we will split them before loading and treat them as separate pallets in A4 and T5. Before we lock this as our standard, does anyone see a need for an extra color, for example for dangerous goods, or can we handle that via symbols and the safety checklist in A3?

For dangerous goods, I would prefer a clear visual. Maybe we can keep the same color scheme but add a big hazard pictogram sticker as per A3, so we do not run out of colors. That way, the label format in A2 stays simple, and we rely on the safety symbols for the extra warning. I can help stick those during packing.

Agree with using hazard pictograms instead of another color. It keeps A2 manageable and aligns with the safety checklist in A3. From my side, the label format and color coding you described in A2 are good to go. Once we confirm, we should print a quick one-page guide and share it in the channel so everyone uses the same approach during T4 and T5.

No extra color needed from my side. As long as red is reserved for metal line parts and we have the machine ID and section on the label, I am fine. I will make sure A5 references the same label format so there is no mismatch when we follow T6 and T8.

Ok, then we will keep the three colors and use hazard pictograms for dangerous goods. I will mark the current version of A2 as the final label format and color coding for this move. This will be our reference for all packing and labeling under T4 and for how we record pallets and crates in A4 and T5.

On the inventory cut-off, can we be explicit about the time? For example, finish all counts in A4 for the first weekend areas by Thursday 16:00, then use Friday only for corrections and sealing pallets, and no more changes after Friday 16:00 as per the schedule in A1 and T2. That would give us a clear line between counting and moving for T5.

I like that structure. Thursday 16:00 as the target to complete counts in A4 for the weekend scope, Friday as a buffer for any discrepancies, and Friday 16:00 as the final freeze before we start move-only. It matches the schedule we set in A1 and gives T5 a clear boundary.

Works for me too. Having Thursday as the main counting day and Friday as a buffer will help avoid last-minute rush. I will plan to support counts in the more complex aisles so we can hit the Thursday 16:00 target in A4 for T5.

Then we will set the cut-off for completing pre-move inventory in A4 as follows: for each weekend scope, counts completed by Thursday 16:00, corrections on Friday, and final freeze at Friday 16:00 before we switch to move-only as per A1 and T2. I will document this in A4 and T5 so everyone is aligned.

threads.thread_goal: Clarify safety rules and hazard controls for heavy and dangerous goods.

messages.text: I want to raise a concern about handling the dangerous goods batch in aisle D during the move. The aisle is already tight, and with staging pallets for the metal line move, I am worried about having enough space for forklifts and spotters. Looking at the draft Safety and Hazard Checklist in A3 for T3, I see general PPE and lifting points, but not much about restricted zones or extra spotters for specific loads. Also, how do we want to log any near misses or issues in A6 during T7 so we can review them later?

Good that you brought this up. In A3, I drafted sections on PPE, lifting techniques and dangerous goods handling, but you are right that we need clearer rules for tight aisles and restricted zones. I propose we add a specific checklist item for aisle D: only one forklift at a time, mandatory spotter for any dangerous goods pallet, and a temporary no-walk zone marked with cones and tape during loading. For A6, we can log any deviation from A3, plus near misses, with a short description and time so we can review after each T7 window.

I support adding those rules. We should also align the staging plan in A1 and T2 so we do not park any pallets in the cross-aisle near D while dangerous goods are being moved. That way, the spotter has a clear line of sight. I can help refine A3 to include a simple matrix of which loads require extra spotters or restricted zones, based on weight and hazard class.

For the checklist in A3, could we add a quick reminder about checking pallet condition before lifting dangerous goods? I have seen broken boards cause sudden shifts. Maybe a line that says: inspect pallet deck and blocks, and if in doubt, re-stack before moving. That would help during T7 when we are under time pressure.

From the metal line side, we will also be moving heavy machine parts through some of those areas. I suggest we mark a dedicated corridor for machine parts in A1 and note in A3 that any crossing between dangerous goods and machine parts moves must be coordinated by the on-site lead. For very heavy or awkward loads, we should require two spotters, one on each side, and possibly a short stop of other traffic in that zone.

The one-forklift rule and no-walk zone in aisle D sound good. I just want to be sure we have enough people to act as spotters when needed. Maybe in A3 we can specify that for dangerous goods and machine parts, the spotter cannot be the driver, and we plan staffing in A1 and T2 accordingly. For A6, I can help log any near misses I see during my shifts.

I have updated A3 with: one forklift at a time in aisle D, mandatory spotter for all dangerous goods and machine parts, spotter must be a separate person from the driver, and temporary restricted zones marked with cones and tape. I also added pallet condition checks and the rule that any crossing between dangerous goods and machine parts moves must be coordinated by the on-site lead. For staffing, I will reflect the need for spotters in A1 and T2 so we do not under-allocate people.

We also need to be clear on which loads require additional spotters or restricted access zones beyond the basic rule. I propose we define three categories in A3: standard loads (no extra spotter), heavy loads over a certain weight or with high center of gravity (one spotter), and dangerous goods or machine parts in tight aisles (two spotters and restricted zone). We can base the weight thresholds on what our forklifts handle safely and get a quick validation from the health and safety officer.

I like the three categories. It is easy to remember on the floor. Maybe we can add a simple symbol on the move plan in A1 or on the pallet labels from A2 to show which category a load is in, so drivers know when they must wait for a spotter before moving.

For the metal line, most machine parts will fall into the highest category: two spotters and restricted zone, especially when we move long or tall components. I will list those parts in T6 and T8 and reference the highest category in A3 so there is no doubt.

The categories make sense. I just want to be sure we do not slow down too much by overusing the highest category. Maybe we can limit the two-spotter rule to dangerous goods in tight aisles and the heaviest or most unstable machine parts, and keep one spotter for the rest. That way, we still follow A3 but keep T7 moving.

Agreed, we should be specific. I adjusted A3 so that two spotters and restricted zones apply to: dangerous goods in aisle D and any other tight aisles, and the heaviest or most unstable machine parts as listed by @326777 in T6 and T8. All other dangerous goods and heavy loads get one spotter. I will send this version of A3 to the health and safety officer for review and sign-off before we start T7.

Once we get the health and safety officer confirmation, I suggest we treat this version of A3 as final for the move. We can print it and do a short briefing before each window, and use A6 to log any deviations or incidents so we can review them in the post-move thread.

The health and safety officer has now reviewed and approved the updated A3 with the aisle D rules, spotter requirements and load categories. We will use this as the safety checklist for all move activities under T7. I will mark A3 as final for this project and share printed copies before the first weekend.

To recap which loads need extra controls: standard pallets follow normal rules, heavy pallets and non-dangerous awkward loads get one spotter, and dangerous goods in tight aisles plus the heaviest or unstable machine parts get two spotters and restricted zones as per A3. That should be clear enough for drivers and spotters during T7.

Yes, and we will also mark the highest category loads in the move plan and, where possible, on the pallet labels so they are easy to identify. During the pre-window safety briefings, we can walk through a few examples so everyone knows what to expect.

Then we are aligned: the loads requiring additional spotters or restricted access zones are exactly those defined in the highest category in A3, plus any others the on-site lead flags during the shift. I will note this explicitly in the move instructions so there is no ambiguity on the floor.

threads.thread_goal: Coordinate metal drawing line shutdown, relocation and test runs.

messages.text: Sharing the draft shutdown and startup steps for the metal drawing line. I based them on the Metal Drawing Line Shutdown and Startup Procedure in A5 and mapped them into T6 and T8. In short: controlled stop and cool-down, lockout and tagout, disconnect utilities, label and secure parts, load and move according to the schedule in A1, then position, reconnect, run dry tests, and finally run product test coils to verify quality and cycle time. We need to confirm the exact shutdown time on the first weekend and agree on the criteria for declaring the line operational again after the move.

Thanks for laying this out. In A1 we penciled in shutdown at Saturday 14:00 and restart by Sunday 14:00. Does your detailed timing in T6 and T8 fit inside that window with some buffer? Also, for the test runs, A5 mentions checking parameters and doing a short production run. We should define what counts as acceptable quality and cycle time so we know when to hand the line back to production.

With the current steps, I estimate about 3 hours for controlled stop and securing, 4 hours for disconnect and loading, 4 hours for positioning and reconnecting, and 3 hours for checks and test runs, so 14 hours total. That leaves up to 10 hours of buffer in the 24-hour window in A1, which is good in case of delays. For test criteria, I suggest we require: all baseline parameters from A5 restored, no alarms during a 30-minute dry run, and then at least two coils produced within target diameter and surface quality, and within plus or minus 5 percent of the usual cycle time.

From the move side, we can align the crane and forklift slots in A1 so that your disconnect and reconnect windows are protected. I will make sure T2 does not schedule other heavy moves through that area during your critical steps. On the test criteria, the plus or minus 5 percent cycle time sounds reasonable, and two good coils should be enough to give confidence before we hand over.

I will be helping with packing and moving some of the metal line parts. In A2 we defined red labels with machine ID and section. Can you confirm in T6 which parts are critical to keep grouped so we do not mix them up during loading? That will also help when you do the test runs in T8.

Yes, in T6 I will mark the critical assemblies that must stay together, like the drawing dies, guide rolls and sensor brackets. We will pack them in dedicated crates with red labels as per A2, and I will note the crate IDs in A5 so we can check them off during reassembly in T8.

On the shutdown time, is there any flexibility if production asks to run a bit longer on Saturday? For example, could we start at 15:00 instead of 14:00 and still be safe? I am asking because sometimes they push for extra output, and I want to know how much room we have before we need to escalate.

If we start shutdown at 15:00 instead of 14:00, we still fit the 14 hours of work into the 24-hour window, but we lose one hour of buffer. I would not go later than 15:00 without approval from production and maintenance, because any delay in crane or reconnection could then push us past Sunday 14:00. So we can say 14:00 is the planned time, with a hard latest start at 15:00 only if both managers agree.

That makes sense. In A1 I will keep 14:00 Saturday as the official shutdown time, and note that any shift to 15:00 requires explicit approval from the production manager and maintenance technician. We will not go beyond that without a formal change, because it would put the 24-hour commitment at risk.

I will also adjust T2 so that no other critical moves are scheduled around the shutdown and startup windows. That way, if we need to use the buffer for the metal line, we are not blocked by other activities.

On the test criteria, do we need someone from quality to be present when you run the two coils, or is it enough if you check the measurements yourself and log them in A5? I am not sure what the usual practice is for this line.

Normally I check the measurements and log them, and quality reviews the data later. For this move, I suggest we invite a quality technician to be present for the first coil, but if they are not available, I can still proceed as long as I record all key parameters and measurements in A5. I will also note any deviations from the baseline so they can review later.

To summarize the test run criteria: restore all baseline parameters from A5, complete a 30-minute dry run with no alarms, then produce at least two coils within target diameter and surface quality, and within plus or minus 5 percent of usual cycle time, with measurements logged in A5. If a quality technician is available, they join for the first coil; if not, we proceed with full logging. If we meet these conditions, we consider the line operational and ready to hand back to production.

That summary works for me. It is clear enough for production and maintenance to understand what we mean by operational. We should share this with them along with A1 so they know what to expect on Sunday.
I agree with those criteria. They match how we usually judge the line, just a bit more formal. I will update T8 and A5 to reflect them and prepare the measurement sheets for the test coils.

Given the earlier alignment in TH1 and what we discussed here, I propose we confirm the exact time window for shutting down the metal drawing line as Saturday 14:00 to Sunday 14:00 on the first weekend, with a possible latest start at 15:00 only if production and maintenance approve. This will be the reference in A1 and T6.

And we will also adopt the test run criteria you summarized as the official conditions for declaring the line operational after the move. I will document them in A5 and T8 and share them with the production manager so everyone is aligned on the handover point.

threads.thread_goal: Review move results, inventory accuracy and lessons learned.

messages.text: Now that both move weekends are done, let us review results and close out the project. In the Pre- and Post-Move Inventory List A4, I have updated the new locations and logged discrepancies for T9. In the Move Issues and Incident Log A6, we captured a few minor delays and one near miss but no injuries or damage. Overall, the metal line is running within the expected cycle time, and the warehouse is operating from the new layout. We need to confirm whether the remaining inventory differences in A4 are acceptable or need follow-up, and agree on the top improvement actions from T10 for future moves.

I reviewed A4 and did some random checks in the new fast-mover zones. Most items matched the new locations, and the few discrepancies were small quantity differences, usually one or two units, likely due to last-minute picks before the freeze. For T9, I think we should flag only the larger gaps for follow-up, like the missing full pallet in aisle B and the overage in aisle F. Everything else seems within normal counting noise.

I also did some spot checks for T9 in the mixed pallet area. The blue labels from A2 helped a lot; I could find pallets quickly. I found one case where the label said zone E but the pallet was in zone D. I corrected the location in A4 and moved the pallet. Apart from that, I did not see major issues.

From my side, the dangerous goods area looks clean. The hazard pictograms and the rules from A3 worked well. In A4, I saw one line where the quantity is off by three units compared to what we counted after the move. I am not sure if that is a counting error or if something was picked in between. We might need the warehouse supervisor to confirm if that difference is acceptable or if they want a recount.

On the metal line, we followed the test criteria in A5 and T8. The dry run was clean, and the two test coils were within diameter and surface specs, with cycle time about 3 percent faster than before, likely due to the shorter path in the new layout. I logged all parameters in A5. We had one short delay due to a sensor cable that was slightly stretched, which we fixed before starting production. No quality complaints so far.

On the inventory differences in A4, we have: one missing full pallet in aisle B, one extra pallet in aisle F, and a few small quantity mismatches of one to three units. I propose we treat the full pallet issues as requiring follow-up with the warehouse supervisor, and accept the small quantity differences as within tolerance, unless they involve dangerous goods. For the three-unit gap you saw in the dangerous goods area, we should ask the supervisor to decide whether to recount or investigate further.

I agree. The full pallet discrepancies are significant enough to require follow-up, and the dangerous goods mismatch should be checked with the supervisor. The rest are minor and probably not worth delaying operations for. We can document this approach in T9 and note it in A4 so it is clear what was accepted.

Works for me too. I can help the warehouse supervisor locate the missing pallet in aisle B; it might have been moved to a nearby bay during the rush. If we cannot find it quickly, they can decide on the next step.

Ok, I will walk the dangerous goods aisle with the supervisor and show them the three-unit difference in A4. They can decide if they want a full recount or if they accept it. I will update A4 based on their call.

Then we will consider the small quantity differences in A4 acceptable, except for the dangerous goods line which we will escalate, and we will treat the missing and extra full pallets as requiring follow-up by the warehouse supervisor. I will document this in A4 and close T9 once the supervisor confirms their actions.

On lessons learned for T10, a few points from my side: the color-coded labels from A2 and the clear cut-offs in A1 and A4 worked very well. Where we struggled was last-minute changes to production orders that affected the freeze. Next time, we should lock the freeze earlier or have a stricter rule about changes after Thursday. Also, the pre-window safety briefings using A3 helped reduce confusion in tight aisles.

I would add that having clear on-site leads for each weekend made decisions faster. For improvement, I think we could prepare more pre-printed labels from A2 with common destinations, so we spend less time writing by hand. Also, a simple map posted at the dock with the new zones from T1 would help new drivers.

From the floor, the main pain point was congestion near aisle D when we had both dangerous goods and regular pallets moving. The restricted zones from A3 helped, but we sometimes forgot to remove cones after finishing, which slowed other work. Next time, we could assign one person per shift to manage cones and tape, so zones are opened and closed quickly.

On the metal line, the main improvement I see is to pre-assemble more of the measurement sheets and checklists in A5 before shutdown, so we spend less time filling forms during the restart. Also, marking critical cables and hoses more clearly before disconnecting would have avoided the sensor cable delay. I will add these to T10.

So far, the top improvement ideas for T10 seem to be: 1) tighten the freeze rules in A1 and A4 to reduce last-minute order changes; 2) prepare more pre-printed labels and a simple dock map with the new layout from T1 and A2; 3) assign a person per shift to manage restricted zones and cones as per A3; and 4) pre-prepare measurement sheets and better cable marking for the metal line in A5. Are there any other items you would put in the top list, or can we focus on these for the next move?

Those four cover the main points from my perspective. If we implement them, the next move should run smoother. We can still keep a longer list in T10, but these should be marked as the top priorities.
I agree with that list. Maybe just add a note to start training new team members on the label and zone system earlier, but that can be part of the dock map and pre-printed labels action.
I am fine with those as the main actions. The cone management and clearer freeze rules will make my life easier on the floor.
No extra items from me. If we improve the measurement prep and cable marking, the metal line part of the next move should be faster and with less stress.

Ok, we will record those four as the top improvement actions in T10 and share the summary with the warehouse supervisor and production manager. The other ideas will stay in the list but with lower priority. Thanks everyone for the work during the move and for the feedback here.
